blocks.title: Separate a logic function from its implementation
paragraphs: A truth function says what output is required. A transistor network, a gate circuit and a storage element describe how outputs are produced over time. Combinational outputs depend on current inputs; sequential outputs also depend on stored state.

The examples below specify ideal switch connectivity in words. They are authored logical models, not reconstructions of a lecture diagram. Device delays, sizing and detailed physical layouts require an explicit specification.

blocks.title: Trace paths to the supply rails
paragraphs: In the ideal CMOS switch model, an nMOS switch conducts for gate 1 and a pMOS switch conducts for gate 0. For an inverter, one pMOS path connects output to high and one nMOS path connects output to low, both controlled by A.

At A=0 the high path conducts and the low path is off, so output is 1. At A=1 the roles reverse, so output is 0. Trace complete conducting paths; the state of one transistor is not enough to determine a larger network.

blocks.title: Construct and debug complementary networks
paragraphs: For a static complementary gate, first state when the output must be low. Build an nMOS pull-down network for that condition: series paths require both controls and parallel paths allow either. Build the complementary pMOS pull-up with series/parallel roles exchanged.

An ideal NAND example has series nMOS controlled by A and B and parallel pMOS controlled by the same inputs. Only A=B=1 completes the low path; every other assignment has a high path. Verify all assignments and check that stable inputs do not leave both rails connected or both paths absent.

A correct Boolean function alone does not prove that a proposed physical circuit meets its constraints. Check connectivity, complements, permitted devices and output drive against the supplied design task. Multiple realizations can be valid.

blocks.title: Read a MUX and a full adder
paragraphs: For a two-input MUX defined by Y = NOT S·D0 + S·D1, S=0 selects D0 and S=1 selects D1. This convention must be stated; do not infer an unlabelled selection input.
A full adder has sum A XOR B XOR Cin and carry AB + A·Cin + B·Cin. For A=1, B=0, Cin=1, total input value is 2, so sum=0 and carry=1. Check the numeric identity A+B+Cin = sum + 2·carry.
Timing follows the longest relevant propagation path under the given gate delays. Logic equivalence does not imply identical propagation delay.

blocks.title: Distinguish transparency from an edge event
paragraphs: A level-sensitive latch can follow its input while its enable level is active and holds its prior state when closed. An edge-triggered flip-flop samples around its specified clock edge. A high clock level is not an instruction to repeatedly resample an edge-triggered element.
A storage cell retains a bit through internal feedback while powered; an SRAM-cell access must distinguish holding, reading and writing. Do not treat reading a cell as overwriting it.
For a timing trace, identify the initial state, active enable/edge, data at the sampling event and any stated timing constraints. Without those details a unique waveform cannot be inferred.

blocks.title: Prove paths, function and timing separately
paragraphs: Trace conducting paths for CMOS; verify complementary behavior for a design; check a combinational block by its stated function; and track prior state plus sampling events for sequential logic.
Practice includes fixed ideal-network and adder checks. Open circuit design and unspecified timing are reviewed using criteria, without a fabricated automatic grade.

cards.prompt: When do ideal nMOS and pMOS switches conduct?
cards.answer: nMOS conducts for gate 1; pMOS conducts for gate 0. Determine an output by complete paths to the rails, not by one switch in isolation.

cards.prompt: How are static complementary pull-up and pull-down networks checked?
cards.answer: Verify the output for every input and check complementary rail connectivity. Series/parallel roles exchange; both-rail or floating-output cases reveal a problem under the ideal stable-input model.

cards.prompt: What does the select input mean in Y = NOT S·D0 + S·D1?
cards.answer: S=0 chooses D0; S=1 chooses D1. The mapping comes from this explicit function, not an assumed drawing convention.

cards.prompt: What arithmetic identity checks a full-adder row?
cards.answer: A+B+Cin = sum + 2·carry. Sum is the low bit and carry is the next bit.

cards.prompt: How does a transparent latch differ from an edge-triggered flip-flop?
cards.answer: A latch follows data during its active enable level. A flip-flop samples at its specified edge and otherwise holds state, subject to timing constraints.

cards.prompt: Why must an SRAM timing task distinguish hold, read and write?
cards.answer: Holding preserves feedback state; reading observes it through the access mechanism; writing intentionally changes it. A read is not automatically a state update.

guided.title: Audit a proposed CMOS design
guided.prompt: Explain how you would test a proposed static complementary CMOS NAND implementation without scoring a drawing by appearance.
rubric: State the NAND truth table: only input 11 produces zero.
Check that the nMOS low path requires both inputs and the pMOS high path allows either complemented control.
Enumerate all input cases for correct drive and absence of stable rail contention/floating output. Different valid layouts are not rejected.

guided.title: Trace only specified sampling events
guided.prompt: A positive-edge flip-flop starts at Q=0. D is 1 at the first rising edge and 0 at the next rising edge. Between those edges D changes several times. Explain Q.
rubric: Q becomes 1 at the first specified rising edge and remains 1 until the next one.
Q becomes 0 at the next rising edge, assuming the stated samples satisfy timing constraints.
Between-edge data changes do not make this edge-triggered device transparent. No waveform geometry or timing margin is invented.
